Photograph: Mike Segar/Reuters Yayoi Kusama Yayoi Kusama, Japanese artist who became a global superstar, dies aged 97 From the 1950s to the 2020s, Kusama produced vivid paintings, sculptures and vast installations that often drew on her experience of hallucinations Kusama – a life in pictures Was Kusama the world’s favourite artist? Tim Jonze and Sian Cain Wed 26 Aug 2026 22.17 EDT Last modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 00.24 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Yayoi Kusama, the Japanese outsider artist who reached superstar status after decades living in a psychiatric hospital, has died aged 97. Kusama died in a Tokyo hospital on 14 August, her company Yayoi Kusama Inc announced in a statement on Thursday. Yayoi Kusama: the world’s favourite artist? Read more “Throughout an extraordinary lifetime devoted entirely to artistic creation, Kusama pursued an internationally acclaimed career as a pioneering avant garde artist whose creative practice encompassed visual art, performance, fiction, and poetry,” the statement read. “She continued to paint until her final days, never setting aside her brush, and continued exploration of forever love and eternal soul.” “We will carry forward Kusama’s wishes and, through art, continue to bring hope and strength for the future to people around the world.” Instantly recognisable by her bright red bobbed wig, Kusama became known for her psychedelic colour schemes and “infinity mirror room” installations, which helped her find a huge audience in the age of the social media selfie: her 2024 show in Australia was the most popular exhibition in the country’s history. Yet she had pioneered many of her enduring themes as a young artist in the 1960s, before fading into temporary obscurity. View image in fullscreen Kusama’s work The Hope of the Polka Dots Buried in Infinity Will Eternally Cover the Universe, at the Museum Ludwig in Cologne, Germany in 2026. Photograph: Ina Fassbender/AFP/Getty Images As well as being a sculptor and painter, Kusama put on numerous performance pieces throughout the hippy era that saw her name attached to scandal. She staged “body festivals” with naked performers painted in polka dots and once wrote to US president Richard Nixon offering to sleep with him in return for an end to the Vietnam war. News of such events appalled her conservative family back home. Kusama was born in Matsumoto, Japan , in 1929, enduring an unhappy childhood at the hands of an abusive mother and philandering father. Her wealthy family managed plant nurseries and Kusama would sit and draw the flowers despite her mother’s frequent attempts to stop her. As a child, Kusama began experiencing hallucinations, in which the flowers would swarm around and talk to her. Her coping mechanism was to draw what she saw. During the second world war, 13-year-old Kusama was conscripted to produce fabric for Japanese army parachutes. She later studied nihonga , a traditional Japanese style of painting, in Kyoto, but grew frustrated with its limitations. Rejecting her planned future of an arranged marriage and children, Kusama left Japan for New York in 1958. There, she fell in with the artist and theorist Donald Judd and made a breakthrough with her “infinity net” paintings – vast fields of impastoed polka dots that stretched across the canvas. In 1962, she sold her first of these to the artists Frank Stella and Judd for $75. In 2014, her White No 28 sold for $7.1m (£5.7m) at auction, a record at the time for a living female artist. View image in fullscreen Kusama next to her Dot Car (1965) in Scheveningen, the Netherlands. Photograph: Harrie Verstappen In 1963, Kusama started making “soft sculptures” – pieces of furniture and other objects, such as ladders, covered with white, fabric-stuffed phallic shapes. They were, she said, her attempt to heal her disgust around sex , which she had been brought up to believe was dirty and shameful. Despite working loosely within the spheres of pop art and minimalism, Kusama was not embraced by the art world. She always maintained that many of her ideas from this period were appropriated by white male artists, including Andy Warhol, while she was written out of art history. Kusama’s work was often centred around the infinite and the idea of “self-obliteration”, a concept inspired by the hallucinations that would engulf her. Talking about her 1954 painting Flower (DSPS), she once said: “I was looking at the red flower patterns of the tablecloth on a table, and when I looked up I saw the same pattern covering the ceiling, the windows and the walls, and finally all over the room, my body and the universe. I felt as if I had begun to self-obliterate, to revolve in the infinity of endless time and the absoluteness of space, and be reduced to nothingness.” View image in fullscreen Kusama’s work Narcissus Garden, which she presented at the Venice Biennale in 1966 without being invited. The work was eventually shut down by the biennale. Photograph: Yayoi Kusama At the 1966 Venice Biennale she continued these studies, presenting her infamous Narcissus Garden, a “lake” of 1,500 reflective balls that strived for a sense of mirrored infinity. When Kusama began selling the balls for $2 each under the banner “Your narcissism for sale”, the biennale moved to close the operation down. Kusama developed a flair for controversy. Her artistic “happenings” were often criticised for being mere shock material, yet their political statements now seem ahead of their time. In 1968, she staged New York’s first “homosexual wedding” in Tribeca and washed a “dirty” Soviet flag outside the United Nations building in protest over the invasion of Czechoslovakia. By this time Kusama was engaged in a platonic yet obsessive relationship with the outsider artist Joseph Cornell , which continued even after she had left the US to return to Japan. She had been frequently admitted to hospital during her time in New York and when Cornell died in 1972, her mental health deteriorated further, with hallucinations, panic attacks and suicide attempts. In 1977, she checked herself into a psychiatric hospital in Tokyo that offered art therapy courses and provided Kusama with the stability needed to pursue her projects without distraction. She made the decision to live there permanently, working each day from morning until night in her nearby studio. View image in fullscreen Kusama at work in her studio in Tokyo, Japan in 2017. Photograph: Toru Hanai/Reuters Although she published several novels during the 1980s, interest in Kusama appeared to have waned almost completely by the start of the 90s. But the recognition that eluded her during her early artistic career finally arrived later in life. In 1993 she created a mirrored room filled with small pumpkin sculptures for the Venice Biennale’s Japanese pavilion and won plaudits for the work. She had first seen a pumpkin with her grandfather when she was 11. When she tried to pick it, it had appeared to start speaking to her, and now it became a recurring motif in works such as All the Eternal Love I Have for the Pumpkins, from 2016. Kusama’s focus shifted towards installations that built on her 1965 work Infinity Mirror Room: Phalli’s Field. In that piece, hundreds of soft, pink phallic forms were arranged within a mirrored room. Half a century later, such immersive experiences connected with audiences on a global scale, with the coloured lights and brightly painted pumpkins providing perfect Instagram content. It was not without irony that an exhibition of hers at the Hirshhorn Museum in Washington DC in 2017 was temporarily closed after someone damaged an artwork while attempting to take a selfie. View image in fullscreen Visitors inside one of Kusama’s ‘infinity rooms’ at her exhibition at Tate Modern, London in 2021. Photograph: Guy Bell/REX/Shutterstock Kusama received retrospectives at the New York’s Museum of Modern Art in 1998, Tate Modern in London in 2012 and Washington DC’s Hirshhorn Museum in 2017. Tickets for her shows sold out swiftly around the world and fans would queue for hours just to be allowed a 30-second experience within her installations. Despite some critics wondering if she had become the world’s most popular artist, Kusama always believed that her place in history would not be decided by the art establishment. “I cannot imagine how I will be classified after my death,” she once said. “It feels good to be an outsider.” Explore more on these topics Yayoi Kusama Japan Asia Pacific New York news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Film Books Music Art & design TV & radio Stage Classical Games Design a better world

https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/12/uae-.text: A senior UAE official called for stronger Gulf security and defence cooperation on Monday as regional governments backed Saudi Arabia following Houthi missile attacks that killed 14 people at Riyadh’s international airport over the weekend.Anwar Gargash, diplomatic adviser to the UAE president, said attacks on Saudi Arabia undermined the security of the Emirates and every other Gulf state.Writing on X, he warned that “we are all targeted” and said failures in collective defence had encouraged attacks on the region.“Gulf security is a shared responsibility that allows no room for complacency or delay,” he said.Saturday’s attack on King Khalid International Airport killed 13 people and wounded more than 300. The death toll rose from 12 after an injured Indian citizen died on Sunday, according to authorities.A separate attack on Sunday killed a Pakistani national and injured 11, Saudi authorities said. Yemen's Houthis claimed responsibility for both attacks.Turkey, Egypt and Pakistan joined Saudi Arabia in a statement on Sunday condemning the attacks and supporting the kingdom’s right to defend itself.The three backed Saudi measures to counter the attacks and prevent their recurrence, provided they complied with the UN Charter and international law, and demanded an immediate, unconditional end to Houthi attacks and held the group responsible for their consequences.Ankara, Cairo and Islamabad did not announce any new military deployment.France also said on Sunday it would continue supporting the Gulf kingdom in defending its territory and infrastructure. Its foreign ministry said a French woman was among those wounded in Saturday’s attack.Iran’s foreign ministry said on Monday it remained ready to help mediate between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis. Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said the Iranian and Saudi foreign ministers had discussed developments by telephone on Sunday.Qatar warns of global energy damageQatar’s Energy Minister Saad Sherida al-Kaabi warned that the wider regional conflict had caused “by far, the world’s worst energy crisis”, affecting the flow of around 20% of global oil and gas supplies.Speaking at the International Energy Forum’s ministerial meeting in Riyadh on Sunday, he expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia and offered condolences to the families of those killed.Al-Kaabi, who also heads QatarEnergy, said attacks on energy facilities across the region had caused tens of billions of dollars in damage and severe volatility in global markets.He urged the forum to examine ways to protect energy infrastructure during conflict and safeguard supply flows.“Energy security must unite us, not divide us. It must be protected, not weaponized,” he said.Riyadh airport closure extendedSaudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation extended the suspension of operations at Riyadh airport on Monday as it continued checks on the safety and readiness of its facilities. It did not announce when it would reopen.The Saudi-led coalition also said on Monday it was responding to a drone and cruise-missile threat against the kingdom. Its statement did not identify the intended targets or report any damage.Almost all scheduled flights at the airport were cancelled on Sunday, according to data from aviation analytics company Cirium.Air France and KLM have suspended flights to Riyadh through 31 October, while Lufthansa Group’s cancellations run through Friday.In Yemen, the Houthi-run health ministry said airstrikes on the capital Sana'a around midnight killed one person and wounded 12. The Houthis blamed Saudi Arabia, which did not immediately comment.
